In mathematics, the '''Dugundji extension theorem''' is a theorem in [[general topology]] due to American mathematician [[James Dugundji]]. It is directly related to the [[Tietze–Urysohn extension theorem]] — about extending [[continuous function]]s on [[normal space]]s — of which it is, in a sense, a generalization.

== Statement ==

Let <math>X</math> be a [[metrizable space]], <math>A</math> a closed subset of X, and <math>L</math> a [[locally convex topological vector space]]. Then:

* Every continuous map <math>f : A \to L</math> admits a continuous extension <math>F : X \to L</math> such that the image <math>F(X)</math> is contained in the [[convex hull]] of <math>f(A).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Dugundji|1951|p=357}}</ref>
or, equivalently:  
* Every continuous map from <math>A</math> into a [[convex set|convex subset]] <math>K</math> of <math>L</math> admits a continuous extension from <math>X</math> into <math>K.</math><ref>Theorem 6.1. in {{cite work|author=James Dugundji|title=Topology|publisher=Allyn & Bacon|year=1966|page=189|isbn=978-0-697-06889-7|url=http://www.southalabama.edu/mathstat/personal_pages/carter/Dugundji.pdf}}.</ref>

== Comparison with the Tietze–Urysohn extension theorem ==

The first version of the Tietze extension theorem corresponds to the special case of the above theorem where the target space L is the real line ℝ. Urysohn generalized this to replacing the domain being a [[metric space]] by an arbitrary normal space. The Dugundji extension theorem is a transverse generalization, replacing the target ℝ by an arbitrary locally convex space. There is another generalization of the Tietze theorem assuming that the domain X is [[paracompact]] and the target L is a [[Banach space]].

== Proof ==

Fix some metric <math>d</math> on <math>X.</math> Consider the open cover of <math>X - A</math> that consists of the [[open ball]]s <math>B(x, d(x, A)/2)</math> for <math>x \in X - A.</math> Since every metric space is [[paracompact space|paracompact]], there exists a locally finite open cover <math>\{ U_i \}_{i \in I}</math> of <math>X - A</math> such that each <math>U_i</math> is contained in one of those balls. Choose a partition of unity <math>\varphi_i</math> subordinate to this cover. For each <math>i</math>, pick a point <math>a_i \in A</math> satisfying
:<math>d(x_i, a_i) \le 2 d(x_i, A),</math>
which is possible since for each <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there is an <math>a \in A</math> with <math>d(x, a) \le d(x, A) + \epsilon</math>. Define the extension <math>F</math> on <math>X</math> by:

<math display = "block">F(x)=\begin{cases}f(x)&\text{if }x\in A,\\\sum_i \varphi_i(x)f(a_i)&\text{else.}\end{cases}</math>

The map <math>F</math> is clearly continuous on <math>X - A</math>. We shall then show it is continuous at each point <math>a</math> in <math>A</math> as well. For each <math>x</math> in <math>U_i</math>, we have: <math>2 d(x, x_i) \le d(x_i, A)</math> or
:<math>d(x, x_i) + 2 d(x_i, A) \le 5 d(x_i, A) - 5 d(x, x_i).</math>
Thus, we have:
:<math>d(x, a_i) \le 5 d(x, A)</math>
and then
:<math>d(a, a_i) \le 6 d(a, x).</math>
Now, let a convex neighborhood ''C'' of <math>F(a)</math> be given. Then, since <math>f</math> is continuous, there is some <math>\delta > 0</math> such that <math>f(B(a, \delta) \cap A) \subset C</math>. Then we have <math>F(B(a, \delta/6)) \subset C</math> by the above inequality, completing the proof of the continuity. <math>\square</math>
